title: Three perfect days in San Francisco, Halloween edition
dek: Lakers at Chase Center, a Castro block party on Halloween night, Día de los Muertos altars from SoMa to the Outer Sunset, and an extra hour on Sunday to spend in Golden Gate Park.

hero.caption: The Ferry Building clock tower at the foot of Market Street, where Friday begins.

intro:
Late October is when San Francisco finally gets its turn. The fog of summer has mostly cleared off, and the forecast for this weekend is the city at its most agreeable: partly cloudy, highs around 60, a slight chance of a shower on Friday and Saturday and a mostly sunny Sunday, according to WeatherBug. Pack a jacket you can tie around your waist.

Three holidays overlap this weekend, and the city takes all of them seriously. Halloween falls on a Saturday, which means block parties in the Castro, Chinatown and the Fillmore. Día de los Muertos starts on Sunday: SOMArts has filled its galleries with community altars for the 27th year, the Outer Sunset's Sunday farmers market turns into a festival, and the Mission's ritual procession, now in its 45th year, sets out on Monday evening. Then, at 2 a.m. on Sunday, the clocks go back and everyone gets an hour of sleep back.

There is plenty else. The Warriors open their NBA Cup schedule against the Lakers on Friday night. SFMOMA has a large Graciela Iturbide retrospective, five decades of photographs from Mexico and beyond, which is a good way into the weekend's Día de los Muertos mood. The de Young has 130 objects from Cairo's Egyptian Museum and the Luxor Museum. This plan keeps each day to a couple of neighborhoods: the waterfront and SoMa on Friday, the Mission and the Castro on Saturday, and the Sunset and Golden Gate Park on Sunday. You'll eat well the whole way, from dim sum to burritos to roast crab.

days.title: Friday: the waterfront, SoMa and a Lakers night
days.intro: Start at the bay, spend the day with photographs and altars, and end at Chase Center.

stops.name: Ferry Building Marketplace
stops.text: The old ferry terminal is now the city's best indoor food hall, and an easy first morning. Get coffee at Blue Bottle (there are two counters), a loaf or a pastry from Acme Bread, which bakes with organic flour, and take it out to the benches behind the building to watch the ferries come and go. If you're hungrier, Hog Island Oyster Company runs a full oyster bar inside. Practical note: go before 9 and you'll have the benches mostly to yourself.

stops.name: SFMOMA: Graciela Iturbide, Between Two Worlds
stops.text: This retrospective, on view through November 29, covers more than five decades of Iturbide's photographs, mostly black and white, of markets, festivals, rituals and botanical gardens in Mexico. It's arranged by theme, not by date, and opens with work honoring Manuel Álvarez Bravo, whom she called her maestro. Look for her pictures of Frida Kahlo's sealed bathroom and the famous *Nuestra Señora de las Iguanas* from Juchitán. Iturbide's own line sums it up: "Photography is a pretext for knowing" (Mission Local). SFMOMA opens at 10 on Fridays and closes at 5; buy timed tickets online.
stops.wiki: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art

stops.name: Yank Sing
stops.text: Dim sum is the right lunch for a museum day. Yank Sing's Rincon Center branch closed in September after 27 years, but the Stevenson Street dining room carries on, and as the team put it, "Yank Sing isn't going anywhere." Order the pork and Napa cabbage dumplings and the scallop siu mai. It's a short walk from SFMOMA. Reservations are on OpenTable, and worth making for a Friday lunch.

stops.name: SOMArts: In Their Name, Día de Los Muertos 2026
stops.text: SOMArts has hosted a Día de los Muertos exhibition every year for 27 years. This year's, curated by Rio Yañez and Bridgett Rex, is about mothering as something a whole community does: altars for mothers, chosen families, and drag and house mothers, alongside personal ofrendas for the dead. It's a moving hour, and it gives you the meaning behind the marigolds you'll see all weekend. Friday gallery hours are noon to 7 p.m., and entry during gallery hours is free. It's closed Monday through Wednesday.

stops.name: Sergeant Ma
stops.text: A new waterfront restaurant on Mission Creek, a short walk from Chase Center, which makes it the best pregame dinner in the neighborhood. The cooking leans Chinese. The Infatuation calls the pineapple bun with tiered duck pâté and spicy mustard nearly flawless, and the Spanish octopus is done like char siu and served with scallion pancakes. There are cushioned seats around fire pits outside if the evening stays dry. Book on OpenTable and ask for an early table so you're seated well before tip-off.

stops.name: Warriors vs. Lakers
stops.text: The Warriors open their NBA Cup group play at home against the Lakers, with tip-off at 7 p.m. It's the kind of matchup that fills the building, so buy tickets through Chase Center rather than counting on the walk-up. If you can't get in, the game streams on Prime Video. The arena sits right on the Muni T line.

days.title: Saturday: the Mission by day, the Castro on Halloween night
days.intro: Bread, the city's oldest building, murals and burritos, then costumes on 18th Street.

stops.name: Tartine Bakery
stops.text: The country loaf is the reason Tartine became famous; it's baked twice a day and can sell out, and it keeps for about a week if you want to take one home. For breakfast here, get the morning bun, the most consistent pastry, with a caramelized outside and a little orange zest, or the ham and gruyère sandwich on that bread. The Saturday line isn't what it used to be, but come early anyway, while the croissants are still fresh from the oven.

stops.name: Mission Dolores
stops.text: Founded on October 9, 1776, the Old Mission is the oldest intact building in San Francisco and the only intact chapel left of the 21 missions founded under Father Serra. Its cemetery, the only one left inside city limits, is the resting place of about 5,000 Ohlone, Miwok and other First Californians, which is worth remembering on the eve of Día de los Muertos. There are restored gardens too, including an Ohlone ethnobotanic garden. It opens at 10 a.m. on weekends; tours are self-guided and need no reservation.

stops.name: Mission Dolores Park
stops.text: Two blocks south of the mission, the park climbs up a slope with the downtown skyline laid out in front of it. Walk up to the high corner on the southwest side for the view, then stroll down along Church Street. On a dry Saturday morning it fills with dogs, picnics and early costumes. From the park, it's about a 20-minute walk down 18th and over to Mission Street for lunch, which gives you a good look at the neighborhood on the way.

stops.name: La Taqueria
stops.text: Open since 1973, named one of America's Classics by the James Beard Foundation in 2017, and named the country's best burrito by FiveThirtyEight in 2014. There's no rice in the burritos here, just meat, beans, cheese and salsa. Order the carne asada super burrito and ask for it dorado, finished on the grill until the tortilla crisps; it's off the menu but they'll do it. Expect a line at lunch.

stops.name: Balmy Alley and 24th Street
stops.text: One block long, between 24th Street and Garfield Square, Balmy Alley holds the densest collection of murals in the city. The first went up in 1972 and 1973, painted by women who became the collective Las Mujeres Muralistas; a second wave in 1985 added 27 murals about Central America, Óscar Romero and the Guatemalan civil war. Afterward, walk 24th Street, the heart of the Calle 24 Latino Cultural District, where the bakeries and shop windows fill up with marigolds and sugar skulls this week. Then head back to your hotel to rest and find a costume.

stops.name: Foreign Cinema
stops.text: A Mission institution where films are projected on the courtyard wall after dark, which suits Halloween night. The Infatuation's favorite dish is the five-spice duck breast with crispy potato hash and grilled dates; start with oysters, which are always on the menu and always good, and the salt cod brandade. Skip dessert, the weak spot. Book about a week ahead on OpenTable. An early dinner like this one is the easiest table to get, and it gets you to the Castro while the party is at its best.

stops.name: Castro Halloween
stops.text: The Castro's Halloween is back as a block party on 18th Street between Diamond and Noe, from 5 to 10 p.m., run by the Castro Merchants Association with local food vendors, merchants and live entertainment. Costumes are the whole point; wear one. 18th Street is closed to traffic from 11 a.m. and the 33 bus is rerouted, so take Muni Metro to Castro Station or the 24 or 35 bus and walk. There's no parking, and no smoking or vaping on the street.

days.title: Sunday: the Sunset and Golden Gate Park
days.intro: The clocks go back overnight, so use the extra hour out west by the ocean.

stops.name: Devil's Teeth Baking Company
stops.text: The Outer Sunset's breakfast stop, a few blocks from the beach at Noriega and 45th. Order the special breakfast sandwich: two eggs, pepper jack, applewood-smoked bacon, avocado and lemon-garlic aioli on a buttermilk biscuit. The line can be long, so come early (your body clock will think it's 9:30 anyway). Take a cinnamon bun for later.

stops.name: Día de los Muertos at the Outer Sunset Farmers Market
stops.text: For its fifth year, Sunset Mercantile turns its Sunday farmers market on 37th Avenue, between Ortega and Pacheco, into a Día de los Muertos festival from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. Expect artisan goods, Latin treats, music, dance and art activities alongside the usual produce and prepared food. Bring a photo or a small token if you want to add it to the community ofrenda, or build a little altar of your own. It's free.

stops.name: de Young Museum: Treasures of the Pharaohs
stops.text: The de Young's big show brings 130 objects from Cairo's Egyptian Museum and the Luxor Museum, in six themed sections. Look for Thuya's gilded outer coffin, a gold and lapis pendant that belonged to Amenemope, a chair made for Princess Sitamun, and finds from the Golden City shown for the first time in North America. It needs a special-exhibition ticket, so book ahead. Afterward, ride up the Hamon Tower for the view over the park; it closes at 4:30. The museum is open 9:30 to 5:15.

stops.name: San Tung
stops.text: A ten-minute walk south of the museum, on Irving Street, San Tung is where the city goes for dry-fried chicken wings, sticky, sweet, garlicky and the reason to come. Add the big, crisp-bottomed potstickers and the three deluxe spicy sauce noodles. It's walk-in only, but the communal tables keep the wait short, and lunch is the quietest time.

stops.name: Ocean Beach
stops.text: Take the N Judah streetcar out to the end of the line and walk north along the sand of Ocean Beach. It's wide and flat and always windy, and on a clear November afternoon it's one of the best walks in the city. With the clocks back an hour, the light goes early; stay for the sunset over the Pacific.

stops.name: Thanh Long
stops.text: Two blocks from the beach, this Vietnamese restaurant is famous for two dishes, and you should order both: the whole roast crab in butter and garlic, which the Infatuation says no other place in the city makes quite like it, and the garlic noodles, a bowl for every two people. Add shaken beef if you're a group. Crab is priced by the crab and isn't cheap. Book on OpenTable; it's a fitting last dinner by the ocean.

stay.name: Four Seasons Hotel San Francisco
stay.text: Twelve floors of a 42-story tower on Market Street, a block from SFMOMA and Yerba Buena and a short ride to Chase Center. Guests get private access to a three-floor Equinox club with an 82-foot lap pool, which is welcome after a long day on foot. Condé Nast Traveler readers ranked it the city's top hotel in 2025.

stay.name: Palace Hotel
stay.text: San Francisco's first luxury hotel opened in 1875 and was rebuilt in 1909 after the earthquake and fire. Have a drink under the stained-glass dome of the Garden Court or at the Pied Piper Bar. It's a short walk from SFMOMA and Yank Sing, so Friday's plan starts right outside the door.

stay.name: Hotel Zeppelin
stay.text: A 196-room boutique hotel a block from Union Square, at the foot of Nob Hill, with a rock 'n' roll, countercultural theme: dark, mid-century rooms, psychedelic bathroom tiles, and record players in some suites. It's on the right side of town for BART from the airport and Muni everywhere else. Readers of Condé Nast Traveler put it fourth in the city in 2025.

events.name: Warriors vs. Lakers (NBA Cup)
events.text: The Warriors open NBA Cup group play at home against the Lakers. Also on Prime Video.

events.name: In Their Name: Día de Los Muertos 2026
events.when: Fri. noon–7 p.m.; Sat. and Sun. noon–5 p.m.; through Nov. 20
events.text: SOMArts' 27th annual exhibition of community altars, this year on mothering in all its forms.

events.name: Chinatown Halloween Festival
events.text: The 12th annual free neighborhood Halloween festival and block party, good for families.

events.name: Castro Halloween
events.text: Block party with food vendors, merchants and live entertainment. 18th Street closes to traffic from 11 a.m.; the 33 bus is rerouted.

events.name: Día de los Muertos + Market in the Sunset
events.where: 37th Ave. between Ortega and Pacheco, Outer Sunset
events.text: The fifth annual festival at the Outer Sunset Farmers Market: music, dance, artisan goods and a community ofrenda. Free.

events.name: Tenderloin Street Fair: Día de Muertos
events.text: Free family street fair with live music, lucha libre, a kids zone and lotería. RSVP recommended.

events.name: Head West Marketplace
events.text: First-Sunday market of local makers, from handmade ceramics to vintage. Free.

events.name: Day of the Dead Ritual Procession
events.where: Bryant and 22nd St., then along 24th St. toward Mission St.
events.text: The 45th annual procession through the Mission, organized by the Comité de Rescate Cultural. Free. Worth staying an extra night for.

know: From SFO, BART takes about 30 minutes to Powell Street on a weekday, 40 to 45 minutes late at night and on weekends; the fare is a little over $10, and you can tap a contactless card at the gate. A taxi takes about 30 minutes and costs roughly $45 to $60 on the meter.
Clocks go back an hour at 2 a.m. on Sunday, November 1, when daylight saving time ends. An 8:30 breakfast on Sunday will feel like 9:30, and it gets dark an hour earlier than on Saturday.

A Muni 1-Day Visitor Passport costs $15 and covers buses, Muni Metro, the historic streetcars and the cable cars, but not BART. Buy it on MuniMobile, at kiosks or on a Clipper card. Clipper and tap-to-pay also work on everything.

On Saturday, 18th Street in the Castro is closed between Noe and Diamond from 11 a.m. until 1 a.m., and the 33 Ashbury/18th Street bus is rerouted. Use Castro Station or the 24 and 35 buses, and don't plan to park.
Expect crowds on the T line and around Mission Bay before and after Friday's 7 p.m. Warriors game.
California law requires restaurants to show any service charge or surcharge on the menu. Read the bill before you tip so you don't pay twice; at table service, tip as you would anywhere in the US.
BART runs every 20 to 30 minutes on Sundays, so leave time for the trip back to SFO.
